idiom_name: two role objects (forwarder/receiver) + name-to-address map + marshaller
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each communication partner one forwarder and one receiver. The forwarder resolves the destination peer's logical name through a name-to-address map, marshals the message through a single codec pair and writes it to the mechanism; the receiver blocks on (or is driven by) the mechanism, unmarshals and dispatches to the peer method named by the message type. Keep the mechanism behind an interface so peers never see it, and keep the mapping and codec configuration outside the peers. Add framing (length prefix or delimiter) and an envelope carrying message type and version; decide explicitly what happens when the peer is unreachable, because the pattern provides no acknowledgement, retry or ordering.
code_sketch:
peer1.send("peer2", Command("reserve", id=7))      # peer -> forwarder
forwarder.route(name="peer2")                       # name -> address (map/registry)
forwarder.marshal(msg)                              # envelope: type | len | version | payload
mechanism.send(addr, bytes)                         # TCP, unix socket, shm, middleware

receiver.loop(mechanism):                            # receiver side
    msg = codec.decode(mechanism.recv())
    dispatch[msg.type].call(peer_method, msg.payload)    # peer method
pitfalls: A forwarder that starts routing, fanning out or reordering messages has become a broker; the pattern is point-to-point only.
Marshalling must produce self-contained data: shipping references or pointers across the boundary breaks as soon as the peers are in different processes.
Without an explicit framing rule the receiver cannot tell two messages from one, and without a size bound a hostile peer can exhaust memory.
Byte-ordering mismatches: peers on different CPU architectures may disagree on endianness of integer fields in the envelope, silently corrupting message type, length or version fields.
Partial reads or writes on stream sockets mean the receiver must reassemble frames; treating a partial frame as complete produces silent corruption.
Connection state machine errors: a forwarder that does not handle connection refused, reset or timeout explicitly will fail silently on transient network failures.
Reconnection logic missing: if a peer restarts, the forwarder must re-establish the channel; without explicit reconnection the application stays dead.
Backpressure not addressed: a fast sender overwhelming a slow receiver (or the kernel send buffer) causes dropped messages or blocking, neither of which is visible at the peer interface.
NUMA placement for shared memory: on multi-socket servers, the memory pages may reside on the node of the creator process; a reader on another node pays remote-memory latency for every access.

Wrong move: trusting the static name-to-address map in a fleet that scales, fails over or moves -> peers keep sending to dead or repurposed endpoints and messages black-hole without any error at the peer interface -> instead pair the pattern with a lookup service/registry, or accept that adding a peer is a redeployment event and automate the map rollout with it.

Wrong move: going brokerless purely for latency without owning topology management -> every endpoint ends up hard-coding peer addresses, firewall rules and reconnect logic, the manageability cost the ZeroMQ brokerless whitepaper explicitly warns about -> instead keep all endpoint resolution and connection policy inside the forwarder and drive it from versioned deployment configuration.

Wrong move: treating a successful send as proof of delivery because the local call returned -> POSIX send() carries no delivery indication, so a peer restart silently drops in-flight messages -> instead add heartbeats plus correlation/acknowledgement in the envelope, or move to middleware that owns delivery guarantees.
